title: Nearest Tube / Subway Station Finder
description: Find the nearest tube, subway, metro or underground station to any place with the Nearest Tube / Subway Station Finder — ranked by distance. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, an address in a new city resolves its nearest station in seconds — and the second nearest, which is the one whose line actually goes where you are headed.
quick_answer: The Nearest Tube / Subway Station Finder maps the subway, tube, metro and underground stations recorded around a place you search or your location, ranked by distance. Search the place, press find, and read the nearest stations — the first question of any city arrival, answered from open map data.

Land, find the hotel's station, ride the right line. The arrival hour gets calmer with the station named.
Nearest first is not always step-free first — the ranking frames the question, and transit authorities publish step-free status station by station.
The closest station may sit on the wrong line for your journey; the ranked list exists so the second and third — one stop further, direct line — are one glance away.
Tube in London, subway in New York, metro in Paris and most of the world, U-Bahn in Berlin: the finder searches the concept, not the local brand.

faq: Does it cover every rapid-transit type?

It searches the recorded station data for subway, metro, tube and underground systems — the family of urban rapid transit. Light rail and tram stops appear where the data records them similarly; tagging varies by city.
Does it show lines and timetables?
No — stations and distances are this page's data. Lines, fares and live times belong to the transit operator's channels, which the station result helps you choose.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — search any address or place name.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
Station names change with sponsorships and renamings (occasionally infamous ones); the map record is one honest vintage of the name.
Does MapBench store my browser location?
No.
The station exists but is not listed.
Entrances and stations are mapped unevenly; a brand-new station can lag. The operator's map settles a specific hunt.
Walking distance to the entrance?
Distances rank to the station's recorded point; entrances can sit a street apart. The map view shows the geography your feet will negotiate.
Which station for the airport?
Rank from the airport's point — airport stations are recorded like others, and the list answers with the terminal's own context.
Night services?
A timetable question — the operator's night network map decides, not this one.
Stations under construction?
They enter the record as they open (or as planned entries in some data). A station you cannot enter is marked by reality at the gate — the operator confirms openings.
Interchange stations?
One station, several lines — the record models the station once. Lines and interchanges are the operator's layer.
